topic.title: Context, Grounding, Eval & Harness Eng
topic.slideRef: M1L2 Slides 6, 13; M3L2 Slides 15–25; M3L3 Slides 2–12
topic.summary: RAG grounding for company definitions, observation flooding vs context collapse, trajectory vs final-response eval, 7 coding eval dimensions, Agent = Model + Harness (+13.7 pts Terminal Bench 2.0).

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.3 Agent Quality | Trigger #8 | M1L2 Slide 13
questions.q: A customer's internal support agent gives a confident, fluent, but generic industry answer instead of using the company's own policy definition. What is the correct fix?
options: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (grounding): retrieve the company's enterprise content at query time and supply it as context
Lower the model temperature to 0.0 without changing the context
Fine-tune a new foundation model checkpoint for every individual user question
Add 50 more unrelated tools to the agent's prompt
questions.why: Per §1.3 & Trigger #8: When an agent gives a confident but generic answer about company-specific facts, the fix is grounding (RAG)—fetching enterprise content at query time and providing it in context.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.3 Agent Quality | Trigger #8 | M1L2 Slide 13
questions.q: During a debugging task, an agent calls a tool that dumps 80,000 tokens of raw log files and stack traces into the conversation history, degrading reasoning quality. What is this failure mode called?
options: Observation flooding (context bloat from massive raw tool outputs)
Context collapse (aggressive summarization dropping a needed fact)
Tool poisoning (compromised MCP server returning malicious instructions)
Semantic routing
questions.why: Per §1.3 & Trigger #8: 'Observation flooding' occurs when the context window fills with massive tool outputs (logs, file dumps, stack traces) rather than high-signal reasoning.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.3 Agent Quality | Trigger #8 | M1L2 Slide 13
questions.q: To save tokens in a long session, a developer adds an aggressive history summarizer. Later in the session, the agent fails because the summarizer deleted a specific port number read 10 turns earlier. What is this called?
options: Context collapse (aggressive compression deleting a specific fact needed later)
Observation flooding
Tool bloat
Indirect prompt injection
questions.why: Per §1.3 & Trigger #8: 'Context collapse' happens when aggressive summarization or compression drops a specific detail (like a config value or port number) that the task needs in a later step.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.3 & §6.5 Evaluation | Trigger #18 | M3L2 Slides 15–16, 23
questions.q: Why is final-response evaluation (or passing unit tests) insufficient on its own for evaluating an autonomous agent, and what complements it?
options: Final-response evaluation misses 'right answer, wrong process'; Trajectory evaluation complements it by grading the reasoning path and sequence of tool calls (e.g., reading a file before editing it)
Final-response evaluation is too slow; only human review can check final answers
Trajectory evaluation only checks spelling, while final-response checks latency
Passing unit tests is always 100% sufficient proof of agent safety and quality
questions.why: Per §1.3 & Trigger #18: Final-response evaluation only checks the end output and misses 'right answer, wrong process.' Trajectory evaluation grades the path (reasoning and sequence of tool calls).

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.3 Harness Engineering | Trigger #19 | M3L3 Slides 2–5
questions.q: What is the core formula of Harness Engineering, and what did LangChain prove on Terminal Bench 2.0 in March 2026?
options: Agent = Model + Harness; by changing ONLY the harness (self-verification loops and context injection) with the exact same model, rank jumped from #30 (52.8%) to #5 (66.5%) (+13.7 points)
Agent = Prompt + Temperature; fine-tuning the model weights improved accuracy by 50%
Agent = GPU + Bandwidth; doubling batch size reduced latency by 90%
Agent = Database + UI; replacing Python with Rust increased score by 2 points
questions.why: Per §6.3 & Trigger #19 (M3L3 Slides 2–5): The formula is 'Agent = Model + Harness' (Vivek Trivedy / Mitchell Hashimoto). On Terminal Bench 2.0, changing ONLY the harness jumped the same model from #30 (52.8%) to #5 (66.5%) (+13.7 pts).

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.5 Coding Agent Evaluation | Trigger #18 | M3L2 Slide 15
questions.q: In the 7 Coding Agent Evaluation Dimensions (M3L2 Slide 15), how are the dimensions grouped, and what are Dimension 1 and Dimension 7?
options: Grouped into User-Facing (Outside: 1–4) and Internal (Inside: 5–7) plus transversal Safety; Dim 1 is Intent Satisfaction and Dim 7 is Self-Repair Behaviour
Grouped by cloud provider; Dim 1 is Billing Cost and Dim 7 is Network Throughput
Grouped into SQL and NoSQL; Dim 1 is Schema Mapping and Dim 7 is Cache TTL
There are only 2 dimensions: Speed and Price
questions.why: Per §6.5 & Trigger #18: User-Facing (Outside): 1. Intent Satisfaction, 2. Functional Correctness, 3. Visual/Behavioural, 4. Cost & Efficiency. Internal (Inside): 5. Code Quality & Conventions, 6. Trajectory Quality, 7. Self-Repair Behaviour (+ transversal Safety & RAI).

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.6 Context Window Budget | M1L2 Slide 6
questions.q: What are the 4 Context Window Budget segments defined in Module 1 (M1L2 Slide 6)?
options: 1. System Prompt + 2. Tools & Retrieved Context + 3. Conversation History + 4. Free / Working Budget
1. CPU Cache + 2. RAM + 3. SSD Swap + 4. Network Buffer
1. Input Tokens + 2. Output Tokens + 3. Cached Tokens + 4. Billed Tokens
1. HTML + 2. CSS + 3. JavaScript + 4. Images
questions.why: Per §6.6 (M1L2 Slide 6), the 4 Context Window Budget segments are: 1. System Prompt, 2. Tools & Retrieved Context, 3. Conversation History, and 4. Free / Working Budget.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.5 Evaluation Prerequisite | M3L2 Slide 25
questions.q: According to Module 3 (M3L2 Slide 25), what is the mandatory foundational prerequisite before you can perform effective agent evaluation (such as trajectory inspection or online eval)?
options: Observability (structured tracing and logging of turns, tool calls, and reasoning steps)
Deploying the agent on bare-metal servers
Disabling all third-party MCP tools
Purchasing Provisioned Throughput
questions.why: Per §6.5 (M3L2 Slide 25): Observability is the prerequisite for all agent evaluation—you cannot grade trajectories or diagnose failures without capturing structured traces and spans.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.3 Harness Engineering | M3L3 Slides 3, 5
questions.q: Google Antigravity is described in M3L3 as 'One harness, four surfaces.' What are the four surfaces?
options: 1. IDE, 2. CLI (agy), 3. SDK, and 4. Agent Manager
1. Chrome, 2. Android, 3. iOS, and 4. WearOS
1. BigQuery, 2. Spanner, 3. Cloud SQL, and 4. Firestore
1. Compute Engine, 2. GKE, 3. Cloud Run, and 4. App Engine
questions.why: Per §6.3 (M3L3 Slides 3, 5): Google Antigravity provides 'One harness, four surfaces': 1. IDE, 2. CLI (agy), 3. SDK, and 4. Agent Manager.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.3 Harness Engineering | M3L3 Slides 3, 12
questions.q: In the Google ADK Kotlin Port case study (M3L3 Slides 3 & 12), what did 4 engineers accomplish in 2 months using harness engineering, and what share of the codebase was tests?
options: Generated 57,000+ lines of code (125,000+ lines changed) in 2 months, with ~35% of the codebase consisting of tests
Wrote 500 lines of code manually with 0% automated tests
Ported the codebase in 5 years using 200 contractors
Deleted all unit tests to speed up CI/CD builds
questions.why: Per §6.3 (M3L3 Slides 3, 12): 4 engineers (3 EPE + 1 Cloud) generated 57,000+ LoC in 2 months with ~35% test coverage / ~35% of the codebase as tests.
